Posts range from single-app deep dives to multi-app roundups, workflow walkthroughs, and developer spotlights. If you're a developer and have an app you'd like me to check out, let me know.</subtitle>

    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/finbar-is-an-indy-gem-for-keyboard-first-users"/>
    <title>Finbar is an Indy Gem for Keyboard First Users</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" srcset="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBKzNPQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--d43265948796601c8971e8eba8e2a9371a8a1b4f/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFMZ0FXa0M0QUU2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--566037cccbef5dec0f18059f150ac6f098af6027/CleanShot%202026-07-15%20at%2012.47.43.jpg 361w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBKzNPQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--d43265948796601c8971e8eba8e2a9371a8a1b4f/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFLVkFta0NsUUk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--b11ebfa34111615cae03143e19175f25060c680c/CleanShot%202026-07-15%20at%2012.47.43.jpg 498w" sizes="(max-width: 672px) 100vw, 672px" loading="lazy" data-lightbox-url="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/blobs/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBKzNPQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--d43265948796601c8971e8eba8e2a9371a8a1b4f/CleanShot%202026-07-15%20at%2012.47.43.jpg" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBKzNPQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--d43265948796601c8971e8eba8e2a9371a8a1b4f/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFLVkFta0NsUUk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--b11ebfa34111615cae03143e19175f25060c680c/CleanShot%202026-07-15%20at%2012.47.43.jpg" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In past lives, my bosses pressed me into using a few complex and complicated apps - mostly Adobe and Microsoft stuff, some AutoCAD. One thing they all have in common is crammed menu bars where what you are actually looking for seldom makes sense and when it does, it's buried three levels deep. Those are the ones that Microsoft likes to use as answers to questions on certification exams.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There's no shortage of specialty apps, like Paletro and automation tools like Raycast, Alfred and BetterTouchTool that try to address menu bar searches. Most of them are good at doing 70% of what it takes but they just never seem to get that final burst of polish it takes to solve the problem. That's where Finbar steps in. For $9.99, you get an app that sees every menu bar option, no matter how deep.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Can't remember the name of what you're looking for? Finbar has fuzzy search.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Use the same commands over and over? Finbar remembers that and surfaces them for you.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Don't use part of the app? Exclude its menu choices from what you see to reduce clutter and simplify things.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If your keyboard skills are equal to or greater than your clicking skills, take advantage of the free trial and test Finbar. &lt;strong&gt;Outline Mode&lt;/strong&gt; is the feature to try first--it transforms every menu bar into a keyboard-navigable tree, like Finder's sidebar. You can arrow through, expand/collapse, and commit without lifting your hands.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If your workflow isn't keyboard centric and you aren't regularly drilling into menu items, you don't need this. Use Raycast or Alfred. But, if your daily drivers include the apps I mention earlier, this should be an instabuy.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;$9.99, one-time purchase.&lt;/strong&gt; Free trial available. Download at &lt;a href="https://finbarapp.com/"&gt;finbarapp.com&lt;/a&gt; or via Homebrew (&lt;code&gt;brew install --cask finbar&lt;/code&gt;). Requires macOS Big Sur or later. Roey Biran--&lt;a href="https://x.com/finbarapp"&gt;@finbarapp&lt;/a&gt; on X--built this on the Unix principle of doing one thing well. It shows.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Finbar%20is%20an%20Indy%20Gem%20for%20Keyboard%20First%20Users" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

One thing they all have in common is crammed menu bars where what you are actually looking for seldom makes sense and when it does, it's buried...</summary>

    <title>Mac Tools Consolidates Your Utility Bloat — With One Catch</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" 800w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBL0RGQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--e75d0ed3971c8ece4c3de397af57e810c24c9ecf/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFLNEEya0N1QU02Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--d936e114f03fdb2f8ce27b5d9aea18b88881243b/CleanShot%202026-07-11%20at%2015.45.41.jpg decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Apple, in its infinite wisdom, buries a great many popular system controls three layers deep in Settings, or worse, leaves them accessible only via the command line. Luckily, we have a community of indie developers who are pretty good at surfacing that stuff, building an app around it, and selling it for $5. An app for brightness. An app for the notch. An app to keep the Mac awake. An app to mute the mic. Then one day your menu bar has 40 icons in it and your login items are out of control.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There's a relatively new, free and open-source app that takes the opposite approach. Currently sporting &lt;a href="https://github.com/ggbond268/MacTools"&gt;over 500 GitHub stars, Mac Tools&lt;/a&gt; folds more than 40 of those functions into a single menu bar icon. It's built natively in SwiftUI and AppKit; the functions run on native Mac architecture, not scripts. Brightness goes through CoreDisplay, audio through CoreAudio, and disk cleanup runs path verification before it deletes anything. That last one matters: a cleanup tool that checks its work before emptying folders is rarer than it should be.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Check out the &lt;a href="https://mactools.ggbond.app"&gt;Mac Tools website.&lt;/a&gt; Mac Tools is available through Homebrew:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;pre data-language="javascript"&gt;brew tap ggbond268/mactools  &lt;br&gt;brew install --cask mactools&lt;br&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What It Does&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The features break down into five groups. You enable the plugins for what you want and leave the rest turned off.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Display Control&lt;/strong&gt; -- resolution switching per monitor, DDC/CI brightness for external displays, True Tone, dark mode, Night Shift, display sleep, prevent sleep, notch hiding, and menu bar icon hiding. This group alone covers what most people buy three or four separate utilities to do.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;System Operations&lt;/strong&gt; -- Stage Manager toggle, system and microphone mute, disk cleanup, Xcode cleanup, eject all disks, empty trash, clear clipboard, lock screen, batch quit apps, and a fix for the "app is damaged and can't be opened" error, which is really just quarantine flag removal with a file picker instead of an &lt;code&gt;xattr&lt;/code&gt; command.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Efficiency Tools&lt;/strong&gt; -- three-finger middle click on the trackpad, a cleaning mode that blacks out the screen and locks input so you can wipe the keyboard, IP lookup, translation, global app hotkeys, a full-screen Launchpad replacement, Finder right-click enhancements, and a zsh config editor.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Monitoring Panel&lt;/strong&gt; -- CPU, GPU, memory, disk, network, and battery with one-hour history curves; keyboard, mouse, and app usage statistics; battery levels for the Mac plus Bluetooth peripherals and AirPods; fan control; and a charge limiter that defaults to 80 percent.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Personalization&lt;/strong&gt; -- custom menu bar icons including GIF and MP4 animations, Launchpad appearance controls, 11 languages, and a plugin marketplace.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The plugin architecture is what keeps this from becoming bloatware. Everything can be enabled, hidden, or reordered, so the panel only shows what you actually use.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What It Replaces&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The point of Mac Tools is consolidation, not feature-for-feature parity with every indie tool it overlaps. Lunar is still the king of independent monitor control, but if you just need brightness adjustment, Mac Tools handles it. If Amphetamine is only in your Dock to stop the Mac from sleeping, Mac Tools does that too. Across a whole set of single-purpose categories, it's a credible replacement for:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;a notch hider&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;a mic mute utility&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;an eject-all tool&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Itsycal-style calendar duty&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;a Stats-style monitor&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="6"&gt;a fan controller&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="7"&gt;a charge limiter&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="8"&gt;an app usage tracker&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;The Catch and a Reality Check&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is a relatively new app. After it appeared on GitHubDaily and in a Medium article, its popularity spiked fast. The developer's true identity is unknown; "ggbond268" is a pseudonym, and the project came out of the Chinese Mac community. The README is in Chinese, though the app itself is localized into English and ten other languages. That's not disqualifying on its own -- I run Chinese-built apps like Qspace regularly -- but it's the kind of context you want before you grant an app broad system access, not after.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And several of these features do ask for broad access. Fan control installs a helper with admin rights. Disk cleanup deletes files. The middle-click feature uses an event tap. Quarantine removal is the kind of thing you want done carefully, not casually. The code being open and the app being native counts for a lot -- that's the whole argument for shipping as a public repo instead of a black box. What it doesn't have yet is a public security audit. Worth knowing before you install, not a reason to skip it outright.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Is This For You?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you're comfortable installing from a Homebrew tap, you like open source, and your menu bar currently hosts a small orchestra of single-purpose utilities, Mac Tools is an easy experiment. It's free, it's light, and the plugin design means you can turn on three features and ignore the rest.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you'd rather pay for a mature tool with a support address and years of releases behind it, or handing admin rights to a young, pseudonymous project makes you itch, stick with the battle-tested standalones for now and check back in six months. Promising and early -- both are true at once.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Mac%20Tools%20Consolidates%20Your%20Utility%20Bloat%20%E2%80%94%20With%20One%20Catch" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>Apple, in its infinite wisdom, buries a great many popular system controls three layers deep in Settings, or worse, leaves them accessible only via the command line. Luckily, we have a community of indie developers who are pretty good at surfacing that stuff, building an app around it, and selling...</summary>

src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBMC9FQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--bec8e7eecce636e597bfba24d270e74c122bca0f/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJZ0Eya0NJQU02Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--8cebb1c2983a7e4106444e274de6ebedc86813b1/CleanShot%202026-07-11%20at%2009.16.02.jpg" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I've resisted the whole category of apps that nag you about breaks, posture, hydration, and eyestrain. Being told what to do by my computer felt like an insult to my judgment.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The reality: my judgment about when to take a break is bad. I lose track of time at the keyboard, I resist interruptions on principle, and by the end of most days I'm running well under 100%. None of that is a software problem until you decide it's worth fixing with software.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I evaluated a handful of the popular Mac App Store options for this. I landed on &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/viraam-smart-wellness-breaks/id6756242904?mt=12"&gt;Viraam&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;The features that actually matter&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Context detection.&lt;/strong&gt; Viraam auto-pauses during meetings, calls, screen sharing, fullscreen video (Netflix, YouTube, VLC), and when you've stepped away from the Mac. This is the feature that makes the rest of the app tolerable — a break reminder that fires mid-screen-share is a break reminder you'll disable within a week.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Six routines, not one timer.&lt;/strong&gt; Eye rest (20-20-20), stand and stretch, hydration, general breaks, walking, meditation. Most competitors in this category do the eye-strain timer and stop there.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Guided audio eye exercises.&lt;/strong&gt; Palming and blinking sessions with calming sound. This is the one feature I hadn't considered before trying the app, and it's the one none of the comparable apps below offer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Quiet Mode, Pomodoro, and automation.&lt;/strong&gt; A toggle for cafés and shared offices, a configurable Pomodoro timer (5–120 min), Shortcuts and Siri support, and Focus Filter awareness so behavior changes per Focus mode.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Local-only data.&lt;/strong&gt; No account, no analytics, no telemetry. The App Store privacy label says "Data Not Collected," which for once matches the actual product.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Sleep wind down reminder&lt;/strong&gt; - Rather than simply marking the end of the workday, you configure how much screen-free time you want before sleep, and it reminds you to wrap up with that runway in mind.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Who this is for&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Anyone who spends long uninterrupted hours at a screen and has already proven, to themselves, that willpower alone doesn't produce breaks. Developers, writers, designers — the people whose flow state is exactly the thing that erases the sense of time passing.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Who this isn't for&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you just want a plain 20-20-20 timer with no wellness scope creep, Viraam is more app than you need. Stretchly or BreakTimer will do the one job without asking you to also think about hydration and meditation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;The competition&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Time Out&lt;/strong&gt; (&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/time-out-break-reminders/id402592703"&gt;App Store&lt;/a&gt;) — free, with one-time supporter tips ($3.99–$14.99, no subscription). Mature and deeply configurable via AppleScript/Automator, but it has no automatic meeting or video detection and no guided exercises. This is a scriptable utility, not an adaptive system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Stretchly&lt;/strong&gt; (&lt;a href="https://github.com/hovancik/stretchly"&gt;GitHub&lt;/a&gt;) — free and open source, cross-platform. The honest choice if you want zero cost and don't care about native polish. It's Electron, it ships unsigned on Mac, and it has no eye exercises, hydration, or meditation content. Does the timer job and nothing else.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;LookAway&lt;/strong&gt; (&lt;a href="https://lookaway.com/"&gt;lookaway.com&lt;/a&gt;) — starts at $19 one-time, also on the App Store and Setapp. The closest real competitor: posture/blink reminders and "Smart Pause" context awareness are comparable to Viraam's context detection. Where it stays narrower is scope — it's built around screen breaks and iPhone sync, not hydration, meditation, or sleep wind-down.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;DeskRest&lt;/strong&gt; (&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/deskrest-smart-break-reminder/id6751417411"&gt;App Store&lt;/a&gt;) — free with in-app purchases. Pairs breaks with posture alerts and an end-of-day "quitting time" boundary reminder, which is a genuinely useful idea similar to Viraam's sleep wind-down reminder. It doesn't do guided audio eye exercises or mindfulness routines, though.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For me, context-aware pausing and breadth of routine mattered than "is it free". Trialing Viraam and LookAway side by side helped me decide to go with Viraam.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Details&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Website:&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;a href="https://www.viraam.app/"&gt;viraam.app&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Price:&lt;/strong&gt; $2.99/month, $19.99/year, or $49.99 lifetime; 14-day free trial&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Availability:&lt;/strong&gt; Mac App Store only&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Privacy:&lt;/strong&gt; No data collected&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;50% Discount&lt;/strong&gt;: Use code AppAddict&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Sxitch&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Sxitch is a variation on the Right-Cmd launcher pioneered by the Low-Tech Guys. Right-Cmd opens a popup; type letters and the list narrows -- "tree-based navigation" -- until one app is left, which auto-focuses. No cycling.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;What I like:&lt;/strong&gt; The tree-based, letter-narrowing mechanic is the clear differentiator versus Cmd+Tab's unpredictable cycling. The free tier includes tree-based switching and themes; Pro adds window switching, a Hide/Quit mode, overrides, blacklists, and priority support via Discord. The developer is responsive to user feedback and has already shipped a list-view feature based on Reddit requests.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Cons:&lt;/strong&gt; May not be enough of a difference from Raycast or Alfred to justify a separate tool for some users.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Price:&lt;/strong&gt; $10 for lifetime access on up to 3 Macs, or $2 a month, cancel anytime.&lt;/p&gt;

    <title>The World Needs More $5 Apps Like NanoClip</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" 480w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBOVM5QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--8874fc7fecd93207827872f5057f9f11ae765da3/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJZ0Eya0NJQU02Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--8cebb1c2983a7e4106444e274de6ebedc86813b1/CleanShot%202026-07-09%20at%2016.16.44.jpg 800w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBOVM5QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--8874fc7fecd93207827872f5057f9f11ae765da3/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFMS0Eya0N5Z002Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--7f04f913d711fb2acbe608efb4bea3a73b00c6b6/CleanShot%202026-07-09%20at%2016.16.44.jpg 970w" sizes="(max-width: 672px) 100vw, 672px" loading="lazy" data-lightbox-url="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/blobs/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBOVM5QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--8874fc7fecd93207827872f5057f9f11ae765da3/CleanShot%202026-07-09%20at%2016.16.44.jpg" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBOVM5QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--8874fc7fecd93207827872f5057f9f11ae765da3/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJZ0Eya0NJQU02Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--8cebb1c2983a7e4106444e274de6ebedc86813b1/CleanShot%202026-07-09%20at%2016.16.44.jpg" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;NanoClip is a menu-bar app combining clipboard history, text-expansion snippets, and clipboard automation "flows." Free/demo tier; Pro is $9.99 one-time ($5 with code EARLYBIRD through Jul 31). macOS 14+, local-first, optional iCloud sync, no account. By Victor Baro. (&lt;a href="https://www.getnano.dev/clip"&gt;getnano.dev/clip&lt;/a&gt;)&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The world needs more $5 apps like &lt;a href="https://www.getnano.dev/clip"&gt;NanoClip&lt;/a&gt;. Before you roll your eyes at yet another clipboard utility, this one is actually three utilities rolled into one, and each can be summoned with its own global hotkey, fully remappable:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Clipboard history (⌃⌘V)&lt;/strong&gt; -- everything you've copied, searchable&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Snippets (⌃⌘S)&lt;/strong&gt; -- text expansion with keyword auto-triggers&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Flows (⌃⌘F)&lt;/strong&gt; -- automations that transform whatever's on your clipboard&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Upfront, I'll tell you that you can get a portion (but not all) of what NanoClip offers from Raycast or Alfred. The developer isn't hiding from that; right on the product page he features detailed comparisons against both of those big-name launchers, plus Maccy and Paste.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I'm a heavy Raycast user, and inside it I keep a large set of text expansion snippets I've been using for years, imported from the OG TextExpander app, which is now subscription-based. NanoClip's snippets can go head to head with Raycast's: they support dynamic placeholders for the current date, clipboard contents, or fields you fill in before pasting.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I also use Raycast's clipboard manager, and unlimited history is one of the main reasons I pay for Pro. Raycast, however, doesn't sync clipboard history between machines, and that's why I'm continually tempted to leave it. NanoClip Pro gives me unlimited clipboard history for $5 once versus $8 every month for Raycast Pro (which adds more than just clipboard history, to be fair). It also syncs history and snippets between Macs via iCloud -- optional, for obvious privacy reasons.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The tools power users expect are here too: search, pinned items, and a paste queue that lets you copy several items and then paste them out in order -- handy for forms and spreadsheets. History captures text, rich text, code, links (with rich previews), images, GIFs, files, and color values, each rendered with an inline preview so you can see what you're about to paste.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Although I write a lot, I confess to underusing the text manipulation tools I already own. Flows might fix that. You get 30 built-in blocks across text, image, URL, and AI categories, including regex extraction, JSON formatting, OCR, image resize/convert, URL tracking-parameter stripping, QR generation, and even Bash commands (direct-download build only). The AI blocks are strictly optional and run either locally (Apple Intelligence or Ollama) or through your own API key for OpenAI, Anthropic, or Gemini.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Comparable apps&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://maccy.app/"&gt;Maccy&lt;/a&gt; is free and open source, the default recommendation for pure clipboard history, but has no snippets, flows, sync, or rich previews.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://pasteapp.io/pricing"&gt;Paste&lt;/a&gt; ($29.99/year or $89.99 lifetime) has the prettiest UI and iPhone/iPad sync, but it's a subscription for what NanoClip charges $9.99 once for.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.raycast.com/pricing"&gt;Raycast&lt;/a&gt; includes clipboard history (30-day retention) and snippets free inside its launcher; unlimited history and sync need Pro at $8/month.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Alfred's Powerpack (one-time, ~£34) similarly bundles clipboard history and snippets into a launcher.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;NanoClip's free tier is a demo more than a daily driver (last 5 clipboard items, 3 snippets), but at $5 through July 31 -- $9.99 after -- Pro is a bargain if you need all its features.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=The%20World%20Needs%20More%20$5%20Apps%20Like%20NanoClip" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>NanoClip is a menu-bar app combining clipboard history, text-expansion snippets, and clipboard automation "flows." Free/demo tier; Pro is $9.99 one-time ($5 with code EARLYBIRD through Jul 31). macOS 14+, local-first, optional iCloud sync, no account. By Victor Baro. (getnano.dev/clip)

The world needs more $5 apps like NanoClip. Before you roll...</summary>

    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/allihat-good-app-hard-sell"/>
    <title>Allihat: Good App, Hard Sell</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" srcset="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBN2kzQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--9d98ec8d59e3ce9873e02a2e5bba20f0cdf9a26b/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFMZ0FXa0M0QUU2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--566037cccbef5dec0f18059f150ac6f098af6027/CleanShot%202026-07-08%20at%2012.03.09.jpg 800w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBN2kzQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--9d98ec8d59e3ce9873e02a2e5bba20f0cdf9a26b/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFLUEJHa0Nqd1E2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--07e515611a6679874685d7606b815d1a3c3eb423/CleanShot%202026-07-08%20at%2012.03.09.jpg 1167w" sizes="(max-width: 672px) 100vw, 672px" loading="lazy" data-lightbox-url="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/blobs/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBN2kzQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--9d98ec8d59e3ce9873e02a2e5bba20f0cdf9a26b/CleanShot%202026-07-08%20at%2012.03.09.jpg" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBN2kzQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--9d98ec8d59e3ce9873e02a2e5bba20f0cdf9a26b/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJZ0Eya0NJQU02Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--8cebb1c2983a7e4106444e274de6ebedc86813b1/CleanShot%202026-07-08%20at%2012.03.09.jpg" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Reviewing software has become a minefield. Post something positive and somebody decides you must be the developer in disguise. Review a paid app and a crowd shows up to litigate every penny; make it a subscription and they bring reinforcements. Privacy-focused readers want to know where every byte goes, and given the state of surveillance capitalism, that's fair. Then there's the elephant in the room: AI. Half the internet bristles at it for reasons that are at least partly justified, while the other half has quietly used it to do things that would have been difficult to impossible without it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;None of that changes what a review is for: what the app does, who it helps, and what I learned from actually testing it. So here goes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;AlliHat&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://allihat.com/"&gt;AlliHat&lt;/a&gt; is a Safari extension by Nathan Kontny that puts an AI assistant — Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, or Apple's on-device model — in the Safari sidebar (&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/allihat/id6760651569?mt=12"&gt;App Store&lt;/a&gt;). Free download, $29.99/year IAP, macOS 14 or later.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;Features&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;BYOK.&lt;/strong&gt; Bring your own key from any of the paid models, or use Apple's built-in model entirely on-device. Communication with the paid models is direct — no middleman — and your key stays on your machine.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Agent Mode (Claude only).&lt;/strong&gt; Clicks, fills forms, scrolls, and navigates pages for you; essentially Claude-in-Chrome for Safari. If you've de-Googled and want to stay that way, this gets you a Chrome-native feature without Chrome.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Per-URL conversations.&lt;/strong&gt; Chats about a page are saved against its URL and reappear when you revisit. In Agent Mode, you can save and reuse workflows for repeated tasks.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;PDF handling.&lt;/strong&gt; Open a PDF in Safari and AlliHat can read and summarize it, NotebookLM-style. It handles scans and tables too.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;YouTube summaries&lt;/strong&gt; via video transcripts.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="6"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Native Safari App Extension.&lt;/strong&gt; 603 KB, no Electron. Global hotkey (⌘⇧C) and right-click actions on selected text: Explain, Summarize, Synonyms.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;Comparable Apps&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://makerstack.co/reviews/sider-review/"&gt;Sider&lt;/a&gt; works in Safari, Chrome, and Edge with a free tier and paid plans from roughly $8.30/month, but it's credit-metered and routes through Sider's servers rather than your own API key.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://elephas.app/pricing"&gt;Elephas&lt;/a&gt; ($9.99/month, $99/year, or lifetime tiers) is a Mac-wide AI assistant that works in every app, not just Safari, but has no browsing agent mode.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://github.com/luyu0279/BrainyAI"&gt;BrainyAI&lt;/a&gt; is a free, open-source sidebar alternative to Sider and Monica, but Chrome-only.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Beyond extensions, an AI sidebar is a built-in feature of the AI browsers (Dia, Perplexity's Comet, OpenAI's Atlas) and of Anthropic's own Claude extension for Chrome. AlliHat exists precisely because Safari has none of these.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;Who It's For&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you only use Safari for privacy or battery reasons and want page-aware AI without switching browsers or paying a second subscription on top of your API costs. BYOK plus a native extension is exactly the right architecture for that person, and nothing else on Safari that I am aware of offers an agent mode at all.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That's the catch: $29.99/year plus your own API bills for one browser's sidebar is a hard sell when switching to Chrome gets you Claude's extension free, and Apple keeps folding more AI into Safari itself. Good app; the pricing math is the part you have to make peace with.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Allihat:%20Good%20App,%20Hard%20Sell" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/18526</id>
    <published>2026-07-05T20:02:46Z</published>
    <updated>2026-07-05T20:04:46Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/2026-07-05"/>
    <title>Developer Spotlight - WidgetWorx</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--png"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" srcset="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBekN5QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--329bc20c334cb2c94217ad1e02802ccc0e4ae537/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJY0c1bkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFKQUFXa0NRQUU2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--788f12962803d73fdeb9038f93be1249bbe22794/ck_thumb1.png 320w" sizes="(max-width: 672px) 100vw, 672px" loading="lazy" data-lightbox-url="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/blobs/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBekN5QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--329bc20c334cb2c94217ad1e02802ccc0e4ae537/ck_thumb1.png" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBekN5QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--329bc20c334cb2c94217ad1e02802ccc0e4ae537/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJY0c1bkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFKQUFXa0NRQUU2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--788f12962803d73fdeb9038f93be1249bbe22794/ck_thumb1.png" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I spend a lot of time watching the free-software sites, and for a couple of years now one name keeps earning a click: WidgetWorx. There are currently 17 "unquestionably niche, but surprisingly useful apps" on offer, none of them more than $4.99. In a throwback to yesteryear, a few are fully functional donation-ware. Every app is signed and notarized. No subscriptions, no telemetry, no Electron bloat.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The developer answers support quickly and keeps the apps current with bug fixes and new features. You can tell he put real thought into each title, and I've used enough of them long enough to speak to whether they hold up. They do.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;My Favorite WidgetWorx Apps&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://widgetworx.com/apps/commandkeeper.html"&gt;Command Keeper&lt;/a&gt; - A searchable, personal library you build over time: command-line snippets, shell scripts, SQL queries, even AI prompts, all a click away. That single click can insert a command or script straight into macOS Terminal, iTerm, Warp, Ghostty, or Alacritty. It lives in the menu bar, but it's useful enough that you'll want to memorize the keyboard shortcut. Once you've invested some time building your library, take advantage of the export (JSON or CSV) as a backup. A lifetime license is $4.99. If you're a try-before-you-buy person, you can use it as long as you like; it just shows a time-delayed nag screen on each launch until you enter a key.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://widgetworx.com/apps/butterfly.html"&gt;Butterfly Collector&lt;/a&gt; - A well-thought-out app for tracking your software licenses, and a lot more than just license keys: version, publisher, category, cost, architecture, minimum OS version, platform, and plenty of other fields. If you use something like Hazel that relies on license files, you can attach those to the entry. Automation fans get 10 built-in AppleScript actions, and there's an import function from another WidgetWorx app, Revok. Once it's populated, you can crunch some sobering numbers on what your software habit actually costs. The nicest touch: renewal reminders, which double as a prompt to re-evaluate your stack. A lifetime license is $4.99, with the same try-before-you-buy mechanism as Command Keeper.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://widgetworx.com/apps/revok.html"&gt;Revok&lt;/a&gt; - I'm a little meta about my software; I keep apps about apps, and this is the one I reach for most. Point it at your Applications folder and it scans in a few seconds, returning an almost absurd 171 attributes. Want to see how many Electron apps you're carrying? (I'm down to four.) Curious which framework a developer used? Short on space and looking for what can go? Revok has a "seldom used apps" category for exactly that, and it'll show you which apps installed login items. The user guide is worth a read for use-case ideas. One caveat: you need the Xcode command-line tools installed to use it. Revok is $3.99, works without a license, and gains features once you buy one.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://widgetworx.com/apps/bookem.html"&gt;Book 'em Danno&lt;/a&gt; - I have the ebook collection of a true data hoarder: 28K titles and counting. I manage my collections with a mix of tools, so when WidgetWorx released Book 'em Danno I imported everything just to see what would happen. TL;DR: it didn't break. Drag your ebook files right in; it handles EPUB, MOBI, AZW3, CBZ, and PDF, extracts the metadata, and builds a searchable database. You can add notes and ratings. If you think Calibre is too ugly to live with, Book 'em Danno covers a good chunk of that ground. Pair it with a free reader like Readest and you've got a genuinely capable setup. The app is free to use, but the developer asks for a donation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://widgetworx.com/apps/notcho.html"&gt;Notcho Libre&lt;/a&gt; - There are some clever apps that put the notch to work, but that's cold comfort if you just want to be rid of the damn thing. Notcho Libre is a recently released free app that redraws your display so the notch disappears, and it does it without invasive permissions. Set it as a startup item and get on with your (notchless) business.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Other Free Apps&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can find all of these on the &lt;a href="https://widgetworx.com/apps/"&gt;WidgetWorx website&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;DoD - Get word definitions on demand with this pop-up dictionary&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Stim - Keep your Mac awake on a schedule or while specific apps are open&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Disk-O - Monitor your built-in storage&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Menu Snappr II - A screenshot utility for capturing your screen, windows, and selected areas&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;Menupedia - Bring Wikipedia into your Mac's menu bar&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="6"&gt;A.B.M. Command - A retro-styled arcade defense game for players who like frantic action&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;DonationWare&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;File Fingerprints - Run hash scans at scale with a security angle&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Quill - A menu bar-accessible notes app&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Paid Apps&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;MountBatten - Apply rules to external drives and disk images before they can mount on your Mac&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Trash Buddy Plus - A shortcut-friendly trash management app&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Unibrow - A task manager focused on speed, structure, and flexibility&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Breakin' - Break reminders throughout the day&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;Developer Q &amp;amp; A&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;How did you get started in app development?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;During the winter 2020 COVID lockdown. I built a Spotify player that ran in the menu bar to pass the time. It leaked memory like a sieve, but the sense of accomplishment and creative fulfillment was addictive, so I kept at it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;WidgetWorx isn't your full-time job. What else do you do?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I'm a Product Manager at Unity, where I lead a small team focused on mobile game monetization. Over a long, unremarkable tech career, I've worked on everything from simple video games and ad systems to Google's contract management platform and tools supporting US national security.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Which developers do you admire?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Double-Click Software, a long-defunct Atari ST developer from my teenage years who built many elegant, lightweight tools. More contemporary inspiration comes from The Low Tech Guys, who make some really well-designed apps.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Which of your apps do you take the most pride in? Why?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I take pride in all of them to a degree, but if I had to choose: Notcho Libre, for being a surprisingly simple fix for the MacBook's notch; Book 'em Danno, because it does a good job managing your ebook catalog if you invest the time to learn it; and Revok, for the genuinely useful insight it gives users into what's installed on their Macs.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;What are you working on next?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I'm trying to work up the motivation to start on Video Cat, a video cataloging app that will share a codebase with Book 'em Danno. That's on top of fixing bugs and adding features to my existing crop of apps.&lt;/p&gt;

    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/the-best-ebook-readers-readest-vs-bookshelves"/>
    <title>The Best eBook Readers: Readest vs. Bookshelves</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpeg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBOWl4QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--75cbdde8b3a54b2d1c99bef30ad067b32b97b4a3/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQ1FBWnBBa0FHT2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--cc87c0fa68191e6a7cb05b7e5f0306bc71cbddfe/74630.jpeg 1600w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBOWl4QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--75cbdde8b3a54b2d1c99bef30ad067b32b97b4a3/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQzdnWnBBdTRHT2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--46346238d62549d9a3e0edd00a9afb52e442b938/74630.jpeg 1774w" sizes="(max-width: 672px) 100vw, 672px" loading="lazy" data-lightbox-url="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/blobs/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBOWl4QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--75cbdde8b3a54b2d1c99bef30ad067b32b97b4a3/74630.jpeg" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBOWl4QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--75cbdde8b3a54b2d1c99bef30ad067b32b97b4a3/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQ0lBTnBBaUFET2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--6b540d5bfcfeca9a1dc6d345f6876757413a9f8d/74630.jpeg" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;TL;DR:&lt;/strong&gt; Apple Books is a storefront that happens to read ebooks. If you own your library, the real choice is between two apps. &lt;strong&gt;Readest&lt;/strong&gt; is open-source, runs on everything (Mac, iOS, Windows, Linux, Android, web), and has the deepest feature set I've seen (side-by-side reading, sentence-level translation, KOReader/WebDAV sync), but it's still v0.x and some marquee features are unfinished. &lt;strong&gt;Bookshelves&lt;/strong&gt; is Apple-only and commercial, but it's polished, ships fast, and pairs a strong reader with a 1.5-million-book built-in catalog. Cross-platform reader? Readest. Living entirely on the Mac and want the nicer native app? Bookshelves. Full breakdown below.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I spend a significant portion of every day managing and curating an embarrassingly large ebook collection. For a long time, I was a dead tree books guy and honestly, I can be talked in to visiting a book store with very little effort, but for sheer usability and utility, nothing matches a digital collection.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I still rely on calibre for the heavy lifting. While aesthetically, it may look like a Windows app from 1996, nothing can match it feature for feature for format conversion, metadata retrieval from multiple sources at once, file management and search ability. Using it as a reader is a non-starter though.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/calibre-keeps-getting-better"&gt;Calibre Keeps Getting Better | AppAddict&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Apple Books&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;macOS has included an ereader, Apple Books, formerly iBooks, since 2013 when it was introduced as a stand alone app in Mavericks, Mac OS X 10.9. But even before that, iTunes offered ebook management. For casual readers who buy most of their books directly from Apple, it's enough. You get a clean, distraction free reading experience, annotation support, world class typography and excellent synchronization across Apple platforms. Apple Books is a storefront, first and foremost, just like Apple Music. Both are designed to get you to spend money. Apple Books also has very limited support for library management and for many file formats.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The real ereader competition&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;While there are a lot of options available to Mac users for a native ebook experience, the top tier as I see it comes down to two apps: Readest and Bookshelves.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Readest&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Developer:&lt;/strong&gt; Open-source community (AGPL-3.0)  &lt;strong&gt;Price:&lt;/strong&gt; Free and open-source; App Store version available  &lt;strong&gt;Formats:&lt;/strong&gt; EPUB, MOBI, KF8/AZW3, FB2, CBZ, TXT, PDF  &lt;strong&gt;Platform:&lt;/strong&gt; macOS, iOS, iPadOS, Windows, Linux, Android, Web  &lt;strong&gt;GitHub:&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;a href="https://github.com/readest/readest"&gt;readest/readest&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Readest is a modern rewrite of Foliate (the well-regarded Linux ebook reader), rebuilt in Next.js and Tauri v2. It has 21.5k GitHub stars, 89 contributors, and ships on every major platform including a web app at web.readest.com. It's technically a v0.x release (currently at 0.11.17), but the feature list reads like a mature product.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Readest's feature depth is uncommon: parallel reading (two books side-by-side in split screen), DeepL/Yandex translation at the sentence or whole-book level, text-to-speech with multilingual support within a single book, KOReader sync, WebDAV sync, code syntax highlighting for technical books, a reading ruler, paragraph-by-paragraph focus mode, and full accessibility support including VoiceOver, NVDA, and Orca.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The translation feature alone separates it from every competitor in this category. If you read in multiple languages or work through texts in a non-native language, there is no real competition.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;OPDS and Calibre integration are first-class, not bolted on. If you run a Calibre library, Readest slots in without ceremony.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is a catch: AGPL-3.0 licensing keeps the code open, but the business model is donation-based. That's fine for now (the project is clearly active), but it's a different kind of bet than a commercial app with a defined revenue stream. The v0.x version number also signals that the API and sync behaviors may shift. AI summarization and advanced reading stats are still "building," and audiobook support is currently vaporware.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Bookshelves&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Developer:&lt;/strong&gt; CPE Verm. GmbH  &lt;strong&gt;Price:&lt;/strong&gt; Free (10-book limit); one-time Pro upgrade ($6.99)  &lt;strong&gt;Formats:&lt;/strong&gt; EPUB, PDF, CBZ/CBR/CB7, FB2, MOBI/AZW3/KF8/KEPUB  &lt;strong&gt;Platform:&lt;/strong&gt; Apple ecosystem only (Mac, iPhone, iPad)  &lt;strong&gt;App Store:&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/bookshelves-ebook-reader/id6756848973"&gt;Bookshelves eBook Reader&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I've been using Bookshelves since the day of the first public release. It has always impressed me as the solution for most design issues faced by Mac App Store ereaders. It's 67.4 MB, currently sitting at #24 in the Books category, and the developer ships new features at a blistering pace. The most recent update dropped localization in 33 languages and a batch of reader and comics fixes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The reading experience is the priority here. Paginated and scroll modes, 10 themes, 10 fonts, full-text search, highlighting, and annotations: all the basics, executed cleanly. Comic and manga readers get CBZ/CBR support with two-page spreads and right-to-left mode, which most ereaders skip entirely.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The built-in catalog is useful in practice: 1.5 million free books from Project Gutenberg, Standard Ebooks, the Internet Archive, and a Spanish-language collection. Standard Ebooks alone makes this worthwhile; that project produces beautifully formatted public domain texts that most readers ignore entirely.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The Pro tier ($6.99) unlocks iCloud sync (progress, highlights, preferences across devices), Calibre wireless transfer, OPDS server access, and highlight export. If you're in the Apple ecosystem and already use iCloud for everything else, this is the path of least friction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The main drawback is lack of support for any other platform. It's Apple-only by design. If any part of your reading life happens on Android, Windows, or Linux, Bookshelves has no answer for you. It's also not open source and it's not free.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Which one should you use?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Choose Apple Books if:&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;You primarily buy books from Apple.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;You only use Apple devices.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Syncing notes across your Apple ecosystem matters more than library flexibility.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Choose Readest if:&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;You own your ebooks.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;You use multiple operating systems.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;You run Calibre-Web or another OPDS server.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;You prefer open-source software.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Choose Bookshelves if:&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;You live primarily on the Mac.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;You want a polished native application.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;You care as much about browsing your collection as reading it.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Most of your library consists of DRM-free EPUB files.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=The%20Best%20eBook%20Readers:%20Readest%20vs.%20Bookshelves" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>TL;DR: Apple Books is a storefront that happens to read ebooks. If you own your library, the real choice is between two apps. Readest is open-source, runs on everything (Mac, iOS, Windows, Linux, Android, web), and has the deepest feature set I've seen (side-by-side reading, sentence-level translation, KOReader/WebDAV sync), but...</summary>

    <title>Variations on a Theme: Five Recent Cmd+Tab Interpretations</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpeg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" 800w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBOHl4QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--d9fae69684072d1b1ea7823c76ec79725ee755d5/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQzZBTnBBdWdET2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--ce0692144ece9d081d30d097acdcbb7d89cac61c/15191.jpeg 1000w" sizes="(max-width: 672px) 100vw, 672px" loading="lazy" data-lightbox-url="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/blobs/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBOHl4QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--d9fae69684072d1b1ea7823c76ec79725ee755d5/15191.jpeg" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Apple's Cmd+Tab has real blind spots. It works on apps, not windows. It doesn't know about Spaces. It has no search, fuzzy or otherwise. Several independent developers have recently taken a crack at fixing it, each with a different idea of what "better" means. I'm not picking a winner here -- just laying out what each one gets right and where it falls short, in case you want to try one yourself.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;GroupCtrl -- Free, Open Source (GPL-3.0)&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead of assigning a different hotkey to each app, GroupCtrl walks you through building app groups that match your actual workflow -- Bloom, BBEdit, and Preview under "Files," say, or BBEdit, Sublime Text, and Visual Studio Code under "Text Editors."&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;What I like:&lt;/strong&gt; Git-friendly YAML config -- a real advantage for dotfiles fans, since setup is versionable and shareable as plain text.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Price:&lt;/strong&gt; Free and open source (GPL-3.0) -- no subscription, no paid tier.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Sources:&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;a href="https://github.com/brodmo/GroupCtrl"&gt;GroupCtrl on GitHub&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Switch -- Free, Source-Available&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Switch fixes the "apps not windows" limitation of the native Cmd+Tab switcher. It cycles through every open window -- or just the current app's -- with inline type-to-filter.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;What I like:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Lightweight: 1.7 MB&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Actively maintained&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Licensing converts to full MIT in May 2028&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Can replace the AltTab + DockDoor combo a lot of people already run&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Price:&lt;/strong&gt; Free, source-available (FSL-1.1-MIT, converts to plain MIT in May 2028). No subscription, no paid tier.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Sources:&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;a href="https://github.com/Sanyam-G/switch"&gt;Switch on GitHub&lt;/a&gt; · &lt;a href="https://switch-dev.sanyamgarg.com/"&gt;switch-dev.sanyamgarg.com&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Dory -- $9.99 Lifetime (App Store)&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dory swaps the switcher for a tiny search menu: hold the middle mouse button or the right Command key, then type. It does smart search -- first letter, middle letters, acronyms, even names that just sound similar -- and tracks which apps you switch to most, so your muscle memory builds around how you actually use your Mac instead of a fixed list.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;What I like:&lt;/strong&gt; Broader adoption than the other apps in this roundup. The developer is responsive -- after Dory landed on Product Hunt (where it hit #6), he shipped almost every user suggestion in the very next release, v1.3.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Cons:&lt;/strong&gt; No free trial.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Price:&lt;/strong&gt; $9.99 one-time purchase. No subscription.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Sources:&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;a href="https://segev.sh/dory/"&gt;Dory homepage&lt;/a&gt; · &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/dory-app-switcher/id6746273626"&gt;App Store&lt;/a&gt; · &lt;a href="https://www.producthunt.com/products/dory-app-switcher"&gt;Product Hunt&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Sxitch -- $10 Lifetime (3 Macs) or $2/Month&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Sxitch is a variation on the Right-Cmd launcher pioneered by the Low-Tech Guys. Right-Cmd opens a popup; type letters and the list narrows -- "tree-based navigation" -- until one app is left, which auto-focuses. No cycling.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;What I like:&lt;/strong&gt; The tree-based, letter-narrowing mechanic is the clear differentiator versus Cmd+Tab's unpredictable cycling. The free tier includes tree-based switching and themes; Pro adds window switching, a Hide/Quit mode, overrides, blacklists, and priority support via Discord. The developer is responsive to user feedback and has already shipped a list-view feature based on Reddit requests.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Cons:&lt;/strong&gt; May not be enough of a difference from Raycast or Alfred to justify a separate tool for some users. If you install via Homebrew, double-check the formula -- some users have reported it lagging behind the latest release.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Price:&lt;/strong&gt; $10 for lifetime access on up to 3 Macs, or $2 a month, cancel anytime.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Sources:&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;a href="https://sxitch.app/"&gt;Sxitch homepage&lt;/a&gt; · &lt;a href="https://sxitch.app/compare"&gt;Sxitch vs rcmd vs Dory&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Scopo -- $1.25/Month Subscription&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I really hope the Scopo developer rethinks the pricing strategy, because there's a lot of resistance to paying a subscription for an app that doesn't carry ongoing costs to maintain. That said, Scopo fills a real niche: it scopes Cmd+Tab to the current Space, so a project's windows don't get buried under Slack, email, and browser tabs from other contexts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;What I like:&lt;/strong&gt; 30-day trial, no card required. Native Swift, not Electron -- and it only needs Accessibility permission.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Cons:&lt;/strong&gt; Subscription only, no lifetime option.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Price:&lt;/strong&gt; $1.25 a month.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Source:&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;a href="https://scopo.app/"&gt;scopo.app&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;None of these replaces the others outright. Pick based on what's actually broken for you: free and hackable (GroupCtrl, Switch), a fast one-time purchase (Dory), tree-based muscle memory (Sxitch), or Space-scoped (Scopo).&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Variations%20on%20a%20Theme:%20Five%20Recent%20Cmd+Tab%20Interpretations" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>

Apple's Cmd+Tab has real blind spots. It works on apps, not windows. It doesn't know about Spaces. It has no search, fuzzy or otherwise. Several independent developers have recently taken a crack at fixing it, each with a different idea of what "better" means. I'm not picking a winner...</summary>

    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/18459</id>
    <published>2026-06-25T14:43:20Z</published>
    <updated>2026-07-15T17:12:54Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/mira-makes-youtube-usable"/>
    <title>Mira Makes YouTube Usable</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Markdown&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;pre data-language="javascript"&gt;---&lt;br&gt;title: Mira Makes YouTube Usable&lt;br&gt;description: Mira is a standalone YouTube player that has all the built in features you try to capture with a browser and an ever-changing collection of extensions..&lt;br&gt;date: 2026-07-01&lt;br&gt;---&lt;br&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;

&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;TL;DR:&lt;/strong&gt; Mira is a small (5.6 MB), native Mac app that makes YouTube calm and pleasant: no Shorts, no sponsor segments, no recommendation rabbit hole. It folds SponsorBlock, Return YouTube Dislike, searchable transcripts, optional bring-your-own-key AI summaries, Picture-in-Picture, background audio, and a real Focus Mode into one signed app instead of the pile of browser extensions you have to maintain on your on. It collects zero data, has a long free trial and costs $39.99 for a lifetime license (or $2.99/month). If you only want ads gone and you are fine with YouTune in a browser, Brave or the Vinegar + SponsorBlock Safari combo does that for free; if you want YouTube genuinely de-Googled, FreeTube or Yattee are the better pick. For everyone who just wants one quiet, native place to watch, Mira is worth the money. eryone who just wants one quiet, native place to watch, Mira is worth the money.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Mira: Focused Video Player&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Buckle up. This is going to be longer than normal, but it's about an app in a pretty crowded field that needs lots of boxes checked in order to compete. &lt;a href="https://watchwithmira.com/"&gt;Mira&lt;/a&gt; is a small but powerful native Mac app with unique YouTube enhancements. It also folds almost all the YouTube features you get from using DIY combos (e.g. Brave/Firefox plus Ublock, SponsorBlock, etc) or other stand alone players (Yattee, FreeTube) into one, unified experience.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you haven't spent any time on YouTube in the past year you might not know how awful the experience has become: More ads, more Shorts shoved into every feed, autoplay previews chirping at you from the home page, and a "Continue watching?" nag that kills a three-hour lecture stream the moment you walk away. You can kinda sorta deal with the aggravation by piling on extensions like Return YouTube Dislike and the others I've mentioned, but you have to maintain that yourself and there is always the danger of one part not playing nice with another part.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Mira - Focused Video Player (its official App Store Name) is native on the Mac (and iPad and iPhone). It's not some giant Electron thing you get, unsigned from a GitHub page. It's from developer Nicholas Hershy (Hershkovitz Bros LLC) who shipped version 1.0 in May of 2026 (hence the lack of buzz), and it's been getting near-daily point updates since. It's on the &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mira-focused-video-player/id6767721654"&gt;App Store&lt;/a&gt;, and the home page is &lt;a href="https://watchwithmira.com/"&gt;watchwithmira.com&lt;/a&gt;. Mira has the best privacy policy available, "The developer does not collect any data from this app." (Note: There are other apps named Mira and a video conversion app called Miro. Make sure you are testing the right one.) (Second note - Mira also works with all the big streaming services but for the purpose of this review, I'm concentrating on YouTube)&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;The Mac Experience&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Mira operates like a browser for video. On the Mac it's a full tabbed app: &lt;code&gt;⌘T&lt;/code&gt; for a new tab, &lt;code&gt;⌃Tab&lt;/code&gt; to cycle, using standard Mac shortcuts. You can drag a link in from Safari, Mail, Notes, or Messages and it opens instantly. You can drag links back out to share them. That drag-in/drag-out behavior is Mac-only and it's the kind of small thing that makes the app feel native rather than a phone app stretched to fit a window.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Here's what you get:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;SponsorBlock, built in. Skips sponsors, intros, outros, self-promos, "like and subscribe" reminders, recaps, and filler using the community timestamp database. You pick which categories to skip, you can color-code them on the timeline, and if it skips something you wanted, an Undo toast lets you jump back. You can also submit new segments from inside the app.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Focus Mode. Strips the YouTube homepage down to a search bar, and hides comments and the recommendation rail on a video page. This is the feature that changes how you use YouTube; you go to watch a specific thing instead of falling into the feed.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Set-and-forget UI tweaks. Hide Shorts everywhere, hide Playables, kill autoplay thumbnail previews, force theater mode, default to best quality (up to 4K). Set once, stays set.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Return YouTube Dislike, integrated. A color-coded ratio bar shows the like percentage so you can judge a video before committing.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;Auto-dismiss "Are you still watching?" so long playlists, lectures, and live streams don't die when you step away.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="6"&gt;Picture-in-Picture and background audio. Float a video over your other apps, or lock the screen and keep the audio going.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="7"&gt;Transcripts. Open a video's full transcript, search it like a document, and tap a line to jump to that moment. This works without any AI key and is reason enough to keep the app open if you research from video.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It runs on macOS 14 or later.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;AI with BYOK (but only if you want it)&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I think the AI features are valuable, but you do you. Mira doesn't try to sell you marked up tokens or a subscription that coincidentally tracks your viewing habits. It's strictly BYOK from the usual suspects, Claude, OpenAI, and Grok. Mira's AI Summaries include key takeaways, quotes, an outline, a 15-second version, "explain like I'm 12," fact-checked claims, plus a follow-up chat, all gathered, I assume, from a well-constructed prompt that runs in the background.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The reality: you're paying the AI provider directly, pennies at a time. The docs note a $5 preload lasts a long time because a summary costs a fraction of a cent. The catch is that you need billing enabled on the provider account; a bare API key with no payment method returns an error. The good news is that transcripts work without any of this.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Provides More than Brave/Firefox with Extensions&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I can already hear that guy in the back sneering because he uses Brave. Yes, iBrave blocks YouTube ads for free, it has SponsorBlock-style features and a built-in PiP, and it costs nothing. If your only goal is "no ads," Brave is the cheaper answer, no argument. Mira earns its price by adding features you don't get in a browser. If any of these appeal to you, you need an app.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;It's a single-purpose app, not a browser tab. Video lives in its own Dock icon and its own window, separate from the 40 tabs you have open for work. That separation is the actual product.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Focus Mode has no real Brave equivalent. Brave removes ads; it doesn't strip the recommendation feed and comments to stop the infinite-scroll trap. That's a behavior change, not an ad fix.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;SponsorBlock, dislikes, best-quality, theater mode, hide-Shorts, and dismiss-the-nag are bundled and pre-wired. In Brave you assemble most of this from extensions and settings and maintain it. Mira ships it as toggles.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;One purchase covers iOS and iPadOS too, where Brave's YouTube handling is weaker and background audio is a fight. Mira gives you background play and PiP on the phone in the same app.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;Transcripts, in-app search, and bring-your-own-key AI summaries have no Brave counterpart at all.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="6"&gt;No data collection. Apple's privacy label lists "Data Not Collected," and the AI key stays on-device. Brave is privacy-minded too, but Mira's surface area is tiny by comparison.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="7"&gt;Watch Together sync rooms with chat for up to 10 people; Brave has nothing like it.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you just want ads gone, Brave (or any browser with uBlock Origin) does that for free, and Mira's $40 lifetime price only makes sense if Focus Mode, transcripts, and the all-in-one packaging are value added for your personal use case.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The other free-and-cheap route worth naming is the Safari-extension stack: &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/vinegar-tube-cleaner/id1591303229"&gt;Vinegar&lt;/a&gt; (Two dollars, one-time) replaces YouTube's player with a plain native HTML5 player, kills most ads and the autoplay cruft, restores PiP and background-ish playback, and pairs with the free/cheap &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/sponsorblock-for-safari/id1573461917"&gt;SponsorBlock for Safari&lt;/a&gt; to skip segments. For a lot of Mac users this is the actual default alternative to a wrapper, and it stays inside Safari. What it doesn't give you: a separate app window, Focus Mode's feed-stripping, transcripts, AI, or Watch Together. It's the minimalist's answer; Mira is full-featured.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;The Competition - Free and Paid&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I've tested a lot of apps in this category and the one that comes closest to matching Mira is &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/friendly-streaming-browser/id553245401"&gt;Friendly Streaming Browser&lt;/a&gt;. Friendly is the same core idea as Mira: one native-feeling window that wraps Netflix, YouTube, Disney+, Prime Video, Hulu, Spotify, and the rest, with a built-in YouTube ad blocker, Picture-in-Picture, and some media-player extras (local file playback, brightness/contrast/transparency adjustments). It's published by Sensor Tower, it's been on the Mac App Store since around 2012, and it's free to download with an optional paid tier (a few dollars) for extra ad-blocking and to tip the team.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I wouldn't recommend it to anyone though. It's literally owned by a data mining company, Sensor Tower, and one read through its privacy policy should send you screaming out of the room.&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://sensortower.com/friendly-privacy-policy"&gt;https://sensortower.com/friendly-privacy-policy&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The closest comparisons are the open-source YouTube front ends. Two are worth knowing:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://github.com/freetubeapp/freetube"&gt;FreeTube&lt;/a&gt; is free, privacy-first, blocks ads, integrates SponsorBlock, and runs without a Google account. It's an Electron app and a YouTube client, full stop.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://github.com/yattee/yattee"&gt;Yattee&lt;/a&gt; is the one that overlaps Mira's cross-platform story most directly: free, open-source (AGPL), native, and it runs on macOS, iOS, and tvOS. It routes through Invidious/Piped instead of YouTube's own API, blocks ads, and bundles SponsorBlock, Return YouTube Dislike, PiP, AirPlay, queue, and history. If you want a privacy-respecting, no-account, genuinely free native app and you don't need the streaming-service wrapping or AI, Yattee is the strongest free alternative on the Mac and deserves a real look before you pay for anything.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://github.com/diontron/MacTube"&gt;MacTube&lt;/a&gt; still works, but its last release was February 2022.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;FreeTube and Yattee are both excellent and free, so Mira has to justify itself against them. Things Mira does that the open-source crowd generally doesn't:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;It's not YouTube-only. Mira wraps Netflix, Disney+, Max, Hulu, Prime Video, Apple TV+, Twitch, and more in the same window, and you can add any public video site as a custom platform with popup blocking. FreeTube and Yattee are YouTube clients, full stop.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Watch Together with synced playback and chat across Mac, iPad, and iPhone. That's a feature you normally need a separate service (or a Discord screen-share) to get; none of the open-source clients do it.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;In-app AI summaries with your own API key. The others have transcripts and SponsorBlock; none of them summarize.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;It uses the real YouTube signed-in experience, so your subscriptions, history, and watch state are intact. FreeTube and Yattee deliberately avoid the Google account (Yattee even proxies through Invidious/Piped), which is great for privacy but means a different, account-less experience. Mira's trade-off runs the other way: you stay logged into YouTube and get the full account, you just hide the noise around it.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;A genuinely native, signed, current Mac/iOS app from one universal purchase, versus an Electron app (FreeTube) or a third-party-instance-dependent client (Yattee).&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you want YouTube without the tracking, then Mira isn't for you. FreeTube and Yattee are the solutions you want.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Pricing&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Three options, billed through Apple:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Monthly: $2.99/month&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Annual: $19.99/year&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Lifetime: $39.99 one-time&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You get 5 days of full access on install, after which the subscriptions start with a 7-day free trial; Lifetime has no trial. For an app you'd use daily, the $39.99 lifetime is the one that makes sense, and it's nice to see a lifetime option offered at all instead of subscription-only. All three unlock all platforms.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;iPhone and iPadOS, If You're Interested&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Mira is a universal app: one buy unlocks iPhone, iPad, and Mac. It syncs nothing to a Mira account because there isn't one. On iOS and iPadOS the controls collapse into a floating "eye button" in the corner that opens a tool menu and fades as you scroll, rather than the Mac's persistent toolbar. iPad lets you reposition the toolbar to the left, top, or right edge. The mobile versions add gesture controls (swipe up for fullscreen, pinch to crop a wide video edge-to-edge) and lean on an iOS built-in fullscreen player for the custom sites you add yourself, which sidesteps the usual mobile-web fullscreen breakage. Background play and PiP carry over, which is the main reason to want this on a phone: free YouTube on iOS won't play audio with the screen off, and Mira will. Both mobile platforms require iOS/iPadOS 17. One real limitation worth knowing: on iPhone and iPad, a Watch Together session drops if you background the app for more than about 30 seconds, because iOS won't hold the connection open. The Mac doesn't have that problem.&lt;/p&gt;
