    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/18443</id>
    <published>2026-06-24T12:05:17Z</published>
    <updated>2026-06-24T12:05:19Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/regexpilot-regular-expressions-for-regular-people-and-no-ai-hallucinations"/>
    <title>RegexPilot: Regular Expressions for Regular People (and no AI hallucinations)</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--png"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" srcset="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNVd3QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--b8fbdd9b4d59d377536d1c7025e05291ffa10f9d/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJY0c1bkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFMZ0FXa0M0QUU2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--07abfda25ef2a00c826495e6cd0ba2c73185afd9/11711.png 437w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNVd3QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--b8fbdd9b4d59d377536d1c7025e05291ffa10f9d/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJY0c1bkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUEya0NBQU02Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--ec0ec628871a3de79f2c14a211911268263b3e43/11711.png 700w" sizes="(max-width: 672px) 100vw, 672px" loading="lazy" data-lightbox-url="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/blobs/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNVd3QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--b8fbdd9b4d59d377536d1c7025e05291ffa10f9d/11711.png" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNVd3QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--b8fbdd9b4d59d377536d1c7025e05291ffa10f9d/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJY0c1bkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUEya0NBQU02Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--ec0ec628871a3de79f2c14a211911268263b3e43/11711.png" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://regexpilot.com"&gt;RegexPilot&lt;/a&gt; by developer Kristof Polleunis, is an app designed to protect you and your work from the hallucinations and miscalculations AI can inject into the regular expressions you ask it to build.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Not Voodoo&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It took a while, but I finally realized that regular expressions are not the computer voodoo I always assumed them to be. In 2026, even regular (non-developer) users are managing and searching large data sets of movies and tv shows, music, ebooks or even just collections of documents accumulated over the years. If you do find-and-replace in BBEdit, Nova, or Obsidian; clean up messy CSV exports; build filters in Hazel, Keyboard Maestro, or Alfred; or wrangle a marketing list full of inconsistent phone numbers, you are using regex whether you call it that or not.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Regular Expressions for Regular People&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Although RegexPilot was built for people who already know how to build regular expressions, it has turned out to be a good tool for teaching the rest of us a thing or two. The way it works becomes quickly understandable. You describe what you want in plain English, get a draft, and then see it drawn out as a railroad diagram: anchors as start and end markers, character classes as colored pills, groups as bracketed branches. You fix the part that is wrong by dragging it, not by counting backslashes in a text field. Hovering over any node tells you what it does, and watching matches appear and disappear as you tweak teaches the difference between &lt;code&gt;\b&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;\B&lt;/code&gt;, or what a lookahead actually does, faster than any reference page.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why it's Better Than AI Alone&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;AI models are particularly good at writing regex, until they aren't. They fail, predictably, in a couple of ways. They rely on training data that doesn't differentiate between public and private IP addresses or it interprets all 10 digit numbers as belonging to US telephone customers. AI does pattern recognition. It doesn't think.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;AI models also are prone to giving you the wrong flavor of regex. You're looking for something that will work in Python and you get a Javascript friendly version instead. If you're making a living doing this, you can't tell your customers "It worked in ChatGPT."&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The honest fix for both is a verification loop: paste the draft into a tester, run it against the real engine, throw your edge cases at it, watch what lights up. RegexPilot is that loop collapsed into one window. The AI is built in (bring your own key for OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, and others, or run a local model through Ollama or LM Studio), and anything it generates renders on the canvas and executes against the selected language's actual engine immediately. The "did it hallucinate" check happens before you ever paste back into your code. You are not replacing the AI; you are giving yourself somewhere to catch it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Worth Exploring Further&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Although I've worked in tech for a long time, I'm not a developer qualified to speak on the pros and cons of this app for that kind of work. Suffice to say, the documentation alludes to broad compatibility with multiple flavors of regex and promises that per-pattern recognition happens in milli-seconds.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Regular Details&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Privacy&lt;/strong&gt; - No analytics, no telemetry, no account, no email list, nothing leaves the machine by default. The voice dictation runs entirely on-device via a bundled Whisper model, and if you point the AI at a local model instead of a hosted key, the app never touches the network at all. The only thing phoning home is license validation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Pricing&lt;/strong&gt; - RegexPilot needs macOS 14 (Sonoma) or newer; the core app is about 8 MB, closer to 72 MB once the bundled engines are included. The JavaScript and TypeScript flavors are free forever, which for a lot of web work is the whole job. A single €19 one-time purchase unlocks all 21 flavors with their authentic engines, AI, voice, the full library, and every export format. There is a 30-day trial of everything, and no subscription, which in 2026 still deserves to be said out loud. Download it from &lt;a href="https://regexpilot.com"&gt;regexpilot.com&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Roadmap&lt;/strong&gt; - VS Code extension and a Raycast plugin are on the v1.1 roadmap, with a step-through debugger slated for v1.2. Bug reports go to his &lt;a href="https://github.com/Kristofp/regex-pilot-issues"&gt;GitHub issues page&lt;/a&gt;, and he means it when he asks for them.&lt;/p&gt;

decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Activity Monitor is one of those apps you open when something is wrong and then quietly resent. It tells you a process called &lt;code&gt;java&lt;/code&gt; is eating a core and offers you almost nothing else. No version, no path, no command line, no idea which of the four Java apps you have running is the culprit. For a tool that ships on every Mac, it is remarkably bad at answering the one question you actually have: &lt;em&gt;what is this thing and why is it doing that?&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I've spent the last year using &lt;a href="https://process-spy.app/"&gt;ProcessSpy&lt;/a&gt; as my answer to that question, and at this point it has more or less replaced Activity Monitor in my day-to-day. It's the closest thing macOS has to &lt;a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/process-explorer"&gt;Sysinternals Process Explorer&lt;/a&gt;, the tool Windows power users have leaned on for twenty years. That's a real gap on the Mac, and ProcessSpy is the first thing I've found that fills it without feeling like a half-finished science project.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The developer, Robert (&lt;a href="https://twitter.com/rob3rth"&gt;@rob3rth&lt;/a&gt;), tells the origin story better than I can:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;I was juggling several Java apps, each using a different JDK version — and I couldn't tell which process was which in Activity Monitor. All I saw was "java." No version, no path, no details. So I built ProcessSpy — a developer-focused tool that shows full command-line info, version details, environment variables, and more.&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/blockquote&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That's the whole pitch, and it's an honest one. If you've ever stared at three identical process names and had to guess, you already understand why this app exists.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Don't Let "Developer-Focused" Scare You Off&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The marketing leans developer, but that framing undersells it. If you regularly install, test, and uninstall software — if you're the kind of person who reads a changelog for fun and wants to know what a sketchy-looking background process actually is before you trust it — this is for you too. Identifying what spawned a mystery helper, checking whether an app is running natively on Apple Silicon, confirming a signature before you grant permissions: that's power-user work, not just developer work.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Features That Earn Their Keep&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A year of updates has turned this from a clever utility into something genuinely deep. The ones I actually use:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Click-to-identify.&lt;/strong&gt; Hit a shortcut, click any window on screen, and ProcessSpy jumps straight to the process behind it. This is the feature I didn't know I wanted and now use constantly. It's the fastest way to answer "what is this window and what's it tied to?"&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The Inspector pane.&lt;/strong&gt; Select a process and you get the full picture: command line and path, digital signature and signing organization, whether it's sandboxed or hardened-runtime, native vs. translated, memory footprint with peak tracking, and live disk read/write rates. This is where ProcessSpy stops being a nicer Activity Monitor and starts being a diagnostic tool.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Advanced Tree View with aggregate totals.&lt;/strong&gt; Modern Mac apps spawn a small army of helpers and XPC services. ProcessSpy groups them, links related XPC services by their responsible PID, and rolls up CPU, memory, and thread totals so you can see an app's &lt;em&gt;real&lt;/em&gt; footprint instead of its main process pretending to be lightweight.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Finished process recall.&lt;/strong&gt; This one is genuinely uncommon. ProcessSpy remembers processes after they exit — their command line, environment variables, and history — and even shows a countdown of how long until it forgets them. If something flashes up, misbehaves, and vanishes before you can inspect it, you can still catch it after the fact.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;History recording with CSV export.&lt;/strong&gt; It logs CPU, memory, and thread usage over time on visual timelines, marks when an app was active, and exports to CSV. Transient spikes stop being a mystery you have to reproduce live.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Multi-property regex search and JavaScript filters.&lt;/strong&gt; Quick search handles regex (wrap it in slashes, &lt;code&gt;/java|node/&lt;/code&gt;) across multiple properties at once, so you can match "java" in the name &lt;em&gt;and&lt;/em&gt; &lt;code&gt;-Xmx&lt;/code&gt; in the command line in one go. For anything more involved, you can write real filters as JavaScript expressions with multiple conditions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Menu bar dashboard and status bar indicators.&lt;/strong&gt; A compact popover gives you live system health and the main-window tools without leaving what you're doing, and the status bar can show CPU, GPU, memory, and disk usage at a glance.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Run Shortcuts on process events.&lt;/strong&gt; You can trigger a macOS Shortcut when a process starts or finishes. Niche, but if you live in automation it opens some genuinely useful doors.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There's also the quieter stuff that makes daily use pleasant: a Version column right in the main table, context-menu actions like Show in Finder, copy path, and search-this-process-online, and deep inspection of entitlements, Info.plist, and bundle ID. Several of those — environment variables, entitlements, the full history features — live behind the paid license.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What People Are Saying&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There isn't much independent press on ProcessSpy yet — it's an indie tool from a solo developer, not a venture-backed launch — but the buyers who've left feedback on &lt;a href="https://rob3rth.gumroad.com/l/yzukse"&gt;Gumroad&lt;/a&gt; are blunt in the way satisfied power users tend to be. One verified buyer, Arie Stavchansky, put it the way I would have:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;I was looking for an equivalent to SysInternals ProcessExplorer for Windows. This is it — it has all the features. I love me a native macOS app!&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/blockquote&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Another, Daniel Jarusch:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;All the information in one clear and intuitive interface — brilliant work, thank you very much!&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/blockquote&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That "native macOS app" point matters. ProcessSpy is built on native APIs and AppKit rather than some cross-platform wrapper, and it shows in how fast and responsive it feels.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Pricing and Availability&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;ProcessSpy runs on Intel and Apple Silicon Macs on macOS 14 (Sonoma) or newer, and it already supports macOS 26 Tahoe. It's distributed as an Apple-notarized, signed &lt;code&gt;.app&lt;/code&gt; inside a roughly 4 MB &lt;code&gt;.dmg&lt;/code&gt;, or through Homebrew:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;pre data-language="javascript"&gt;brew install --cask processspy&lt;/pre&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The free version is fully functional for core monitoring. The paid license unlocks the deep-inspection features (environment variables; entitlements, Info.plist, and bundle ID), the history and CSV export tools, and removes the startup countdown screen the free version makes you sit through.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The license is a &lt;strong&gt;one-time $34.99&lt;/strong&gt; on Gumroad, good for one user across unlimited personal devices, with lifetime updates. That's up from the $24.99 some listing sites still show, so the price has climbed — but for a tool I open this often, and one that's shipped this many real updates in a year, it's an easy call. There's no subscription, which in 2026 is worth saying out loud.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you've ever lost twenty minutes to a process you couldn't identify, ProcessSpy pays for itself the first time it hands you the answer in one click.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;ProcessSpy is made by Robert (@rob3rth), who also builds &lt;/em&gt;&lt;a href="https://restretto.app/"&gt;&lt;em&gt;Restretto&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;em&gt; (a REST client) and a couple of other focused Mac utilities. Worth a look if this one lands for you.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/18418</id>
    <published>2026-06-23T00:32:40Z</published>

    <title>SmoothCSV: Finally, a CSV Editor That Doesn't Guess</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpeg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" srcset="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBeG13QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--b81b48a51e9ed00846ada75675138cba26745e58/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQzRBRnBBdUFCT2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--278b8a01e32dcdca3afe205e3ef51dea30581376/94250.jpeg 480w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBeG13QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--b81b48a51e9ed00846ada75675138cba26745e58/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQ0lBTnBBaUFET2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--6b540d5bfcfeca9a1dc6d345f6876757413a9f8d/94250.jpeg 800w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBeG13QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--b81b48a51e9ed00846ada75675138cba26745e58/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQ3NBUnBBckFFT2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--e45d50b9b1b73d418e1972626cdf4e2159e96278/94250.jpeg 1200w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBeG13QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--b81b48a51e9ed00846ada75675138cba26745e58/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQzBBVnBBdEFGT2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--e886c797e3c002568b28ee93ceff45e0715c1c2e/94250.jpeg 1488w" sizes="(max-width: 672px) 100vw, 672px" loading="lazy" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBeG13QVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--b81b48a51e9ed00846ada75675138cba26745e58/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQ0lBTnBBaUFET2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--6b540d5bfcfeca9a1dc6d345f6876757413a9f8d/94250.jpeg" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you've ever had to search for "how to make Excel quit removing leading zeroes," I have an app for you. &lt;a href="https://smoothcsv.com"&gt;SmoothCSV&lt;/a&gt; won't turn some random number into a date and then refuse to change it back. In fact, it won't format anything unless you expressly tell it to. It doesn't try to be a lightweight spreadsheet; it's a grid editor, first and foremost. It leaves your data as it is, with no helpful "guesses" at what you might be trying to do. That's the pitch, and it's enough to make this my CSV editor for most tasks.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Here to Stay&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The first version of SmoothCSV shipped in 2011. The current v3 release came out last year; it's a complete rewrite built on Tauri, which is why it weighs in under 80 MB and opens a 100 MB file remarkably fast. The dev claims it's 12x faster than Excel. I can't verify that number, but I have some genuinely huge CSV files and it never blinked when I threw them at it. Cheers for speed, and for not being another Electron monstrosity.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;The Features That Actually Matter&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Most of the feature list is what you'd hope for and rarely get in one place:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;A real grid editor with row and column tools: insert, delete, move, hide, dedupe.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Find and replace with regex support.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Filtering through either a visual condition builder or SQL-style expressions.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Multi-column sorting by text, number, date, or length.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;Multi-cell editing, the way multi-cursor works in a code editor.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="6"&gt;A command palette, so you can drive the whole app without hunting through menus.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For those who live in CSV files, it also has extras that make it more than a text editor with a few tricks:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;SQL Console:&lt;/strong&gt; Run SELECT queries directly against your CSV. If you've ever exported a table just to ask it one question, this collapses that round trip into the editor.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Customizable file formats:&lt;/strong&gt; Control delimiter, quotes, encoding, and line endings per file, with rules you can save and apply automatically. This is the fix for the semicolon-delimited, Latin-1-encoded, Windows-line-ending file that some other tool flatly refused to open correctly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Copy/Paste As:&lt;/strong&gt; Copy a range as Markdown, HTML, JSON, SQL, or LaTeX. Handy for documentation or moving tabular data between formats.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Excel import/export, aggregation, transpose, auto-fill, and a CLI:&lt;/strong&gt; These round out the functionality. The CLI lets you launch a file and jump straight to a specific row and column, and &lt;code&gt;smoothcsv://&lt;/code&gt; deep links let you wire it into larger workflows.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Licensing I Respect&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can download and use the fully featured version of SmoothCSV from the dev's website, for as long as you'd like, with no limits. The occasional nudge to buy a license is non-modal on purpose, so it doesn't interrupt your work. Like a few other stalwarts (Shottr and Immich come to mind), it's the kind of app you end up paying for because you're grateful and want to support the developer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Who It's Not For&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It's closed source, though that may change one day. If you're FOSS-only, this isn't for you. And if you're after spreadsheet functionality, look elsewhere: formulas across a living workbook, charts, pivot tables, collaborative editing. This is the wrong tool, and it isn't pretending otherwise.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;See Also&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A few other CSV editors worth a look if this one doesn't click:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/delimited-quick-and-easy-way-to-work-with-csv-files"&gt;Delimited&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.easycsv.io"&gt;EasyCSV&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.moderncsv.com"&gt;ModernCSV&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

    <title>SupaSidebar Boosts Privacy and Productivity</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpeg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      SupaSidebar in Action
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Most technically oriented people who value privacy do so because privacy is, and should be, a human right, not because they have something to hide.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Maintaining privacy in the current technical environment requires a real strategy and almost constant attention to an evolving landscape.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It is no longer enough to block trackers, ads, and cookies. Browser fingerprinting has become one of the primary privacy-violating mechanisms used by companies that want to identify, profile, and monetize you across the web.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;One strategy many people use is spreading their work across multiple browsers. That has a second benefit: it lets you match the strengths of a particular browser to the task at hand.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Privacy and Productivity&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The downside becomes obvious pretty quickly: you take a real productivity hit when your history, bookmarks, and open tabs are scattered across multiple places.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There are several tools that try to help with this. The one I like best is &lt;a href="https://supasidebar.com"&gt;SupaSidebar&lt;/a&gt;, by developer Kshetez Vinayak. He stands out for being responsive, helpful, and clearly invested in fixing bugs and expanding the app’s usefulness. I bought SupaSidebar during the 2025 Black Friday sale and have been using it ever since.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;SupaSidebar operates at the OS level. It is not a browser extension. It is built for exactly this use case: people who use multiple browsers and need a way to consolidate browser context without paying a constant productivity tax every time they switch.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Arc was a favorite of many Mac power users, and for good reason. Although it is still maintained for security, active feature development effectively stopped in early 2025. Arc introduced a genuinely useful way to manage browsing around spaces, context, and workflows. SupaSidebar recreates much of that experience, but does it across multiple browsers instead of inside just one.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The power of SupaSidebar becomes obvious when you take the time to create spaces that match how you actually work. You might have a space for research, one for personal browsing, one for work, and separate spaces for projects that need to stay isolated.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Within a space, SupaSidebar aggregates tabs and bookmarks from every supported browser you have open. It pulls in Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Arc, and others. You get a vertical, organized, searchable interface showing your open tabs across browsers.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If your browser use is simple, the free version may be enough. It supports three spaces. Paid users get unlimited spaces.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;SupaSidebar also has a command panel with fuzzy search across tabs, bookmarks, history, folders, and spaces. It works like a specialized version of Spotlight for your internet life.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Features&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Some of the most useful features include:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Recents tab&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;: shows recently visited tabs across browsers, which is useful for recovering something without keeping every tab open and burning RAM&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Multiple ways to save links&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;: right-click, drag-and-drop, command panel, auto-routing rules, and more&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Notes for saved links&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;: add context to a link without leaving the app&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Browser profile linking&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;: connect a space to a specific browser profile so links open in the right place automatically&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Auto-routing rules&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;: send links to specific spaces or browser profiles based on conditions&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;AI chat mode&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;: integrates with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini directly in the panel, with Markdown rendering and slash commands&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Yes, But...&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;SupaSidebar is still, at its core, a beta app. But it has a clear purpose, it is actively developed, and it solves a real problem that many multi-browser power users have simply learned to tolerate.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The spaces model gives it more depth than simple tab aggregation. The pricing is also reasonable, and the free tier is actually useful.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Free&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;: 0-3 spaces&lt;br&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Pro&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;: $13.99/year with unlimited spaces, early access, and priority support&lt;br&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Lifetime&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;: $34.99 one-time purchase, 5 devices, lifetime updates&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Use &lt;code&gt;BETA30&lt;/code&gt; as a discount code for 30% off both paid options.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There are bugs and rough edges. I have seen tab synchronization inconsistencies, occasional lag when opening folders, and occasional page reloads when clicking tabs. The command panel also has some edge-case quirks around keyboard navigation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But even with those issues, SupaSidebar is one of the more useful workflow apps I have added to my Mac setup recently.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you stick with one browser for everything, you probably will not get much out of it. But if you live across Safari, Firefox, Chrome, Arc, and browser profiles, SupaSidebar fills a gap that Apple, Google, and Mozilla have not bothered to solve.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=SupaSidebar%20Boosts%20Privacy%20and%20Productivity" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>Most technically oriented people who value privacy do so because privacy is, and should be, a human right, not because they have something to hide.

Maintaining privacy in the current technical environment requires a real strategy and almost constant attention to an evolving landscape.

It is no longer enough to...</summary>

&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://cacheout.app/"&gt;Cache Out&lt;/a&gt;, a free new single-purpose utility from veteran Mac developer Jim Mitchell, fits right into an app category that is severely underrepresented - utilities that work across multiple browsers from a single interface.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What It Does&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Cache Out's superpower is selective data removal from a variety of popular macOS browsers with the click of a single button. It removes five categories of information - &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;cache, history, downloads, favicons, and cookies&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. You select the browsers you want cleared from a list. You select the categories of data to remove. Then, you click a single button and BOOM. It's done. After the files are removed, you aren't left in the dark about what happened since you get a report on the number of files and MBs that were removed.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There are currently seven supported browsers:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Safari&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Chrome&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Firefox&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Edge&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Brave&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Opera&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Orion&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I'd like to see a few more on the list, including Vivaldi, Arc, and Atlas. Thankfully, Mitchell indicates that more browsers are coming.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Cache Out punches all the right buttons for a privacy-focused app. It doesn't phone home or collect analytics. It doesn't require an account or registration. It's Apple-notarized. Everything happens on your machine.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why You Need It&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Don't think that an app like this is the ultimate Boss Button. Most corporate-owned computers track Internet traffic in real time, so your IT department can still track your history if this is your only precaution. Still, most undermanned and overworked support workers don't care where you go as a general rule. Likewise, your home ISP can track your DNS requests for almost every site you visit unless you use a no-log VPN or a service like NextDNS that offers name resolution over HTTPS. Even then, you have to be savvy enough to set it up correctly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Still, there are a lot of reasons for running clean browsers. In a world where browser fingerprinting is maximally invasive and pervasive, one defense is using multiple browsers to make yourself harder to track for the data scrapers of the world. You'll quickly build up GBs of data for almost every browser you use. If you're stuck with a small hard drive you can't upgrade (like my brand-new M4 Mac Mini's 256GB), you always have to be careful with space. Cache Out is the perfect app to do that.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Also, many countries, including my own, are seeing a rollback of civil liberties. To make matters worse, areas where people travel with their computers offer less privacy than you'd have at home. If you gave the slightest concern about the TSA, ICE, or the CBP looking through your browser history, use Cache Out before you travel.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;2026-06-13 Update&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Cache Out has been updated to v1.3.1, adding several new features:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;New &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Preview before cleaning&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; option: see exactly which files and download-history rows would be removed, and confirm, before anything is deleted.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;New &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Move to Trash instead of deleting&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; option, so cleared files are recoverable.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Each browser card now shows its &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;reclaimable size&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; in the header, calculated at launch.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;New &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Clean default profile only&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; preference for multi-profile browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Opera, Brave).&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Clearing browsing history now also clears the &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;“Recently Closed”&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; tabs and windows that browsers restore from session data.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Added &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;French localization&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Hardened the deletion safety checks against symlink and path-traversal escapes.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Other Cross Browser Utilities&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Here are utilities that operate across multiple browsers on macOS:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;History &amp;amp; Data Aggregation&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/historyhound-a-must-have-research-tool-1"&gt;HistoryHound a Must Have Research Tool | AppAddict&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;St. Clair Software&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; — Indexes and searches browsing history from multiple browsers (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, and more) in one place. Lets you do full-text searches across all your browser histories simultaneously. Useful for finding pages you visited without remembering which browser you used.&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Macro &amp;amp; Automation Tools&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/keyboard-maestro-the-app-that-makes-everything-better-tips-for-the-for-the-automation-curious"&gt;Keyboard Maestro, The App That Makes Everything Better - Tips for the Automation Curious | AppAddict&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Stairways Software&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; — A powerful macro utility that can trigger actions in any browser. You can build macros that work in Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Arc, and others — filling forms, clicking elements, navigating pages, or switching between browsers automatically.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.alfredapp.com/"&gt;Alfred&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Running with Crayons&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; — Launcher and automation tool with workflows that can interact with multiple browsers. Can open URLs in a chosen browser, search history, and trigger browser-based actions via custom workflows.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/how-to-get-the-most-from-raycast"&gt;How to Get The Most from Raycast | AppAddict&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;A launcher and productivity tool with extensions for Chrome, Safari, Firefox, and Arc. Extensions let you search tabs, bookmarks, and history across browsers from a single interface.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Password Managers (Cross-Browser)&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://1password.com/"&gt;1Password&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;Works via browser extensions in Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Brave. The Mac app itself manages credentials centrally regardless of which browser you use.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://bitwarden.com/"&gt;Bitwarden&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;Open-source password manager with extensions for virtually every major browser. The Mac desktop app serves as a central vault across all of them.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Ad Blocking &amp;amp; Privacy (System-Wide)&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://adguard.com/en/adguard-mac/overview.html"&gt;AdGuard for Mac&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;Filters ads and trackers at the system level, meaning it works across &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;all&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; browsers without needing individual extensions installed in each one.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.obdev.at/products/littlesnitch/"&gt;Little Snitch&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Objective Development&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; — Network monitor and firewall that works at the OS level, so it monitors and controls outgoing connections from any browser equally.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Developer / Inspection Tools&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://proxyman.io/"&gt;Proxyman&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;A macOS proxy tool that intercepts HTTP/HTTPS traffic from any browser (or app). Useful for debugging web traffic regardless of which browser made the request.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.charlesproxy.com/"&gt;Charles Proxy&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;Similar to Proxyman — a web debugging proxy that captures traffic from all browsers at the network level.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Bookmark Management&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/raindrop-io-gets-a-significant-new-feature"&gt;Raindrop.io Gets a Significant New Feature | AppAddict&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;Cross-browser bookmark manager with extensions for all major browsers. Centralizes bookmarks saved from any browser into one organized collection.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/goodlinks"&gt;GoodLinks | AppAddict&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;Read-later and bookmarking app with Safari extension built-in and support for sharing from other browsers via the share sheet.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;
